svg.title: Page latch and transaction lock protect different objects for different lifetimes
svg.desc: Two side-by-side panels. The page latch, owned by the page buffer, protects the resident bytes of one BCB and frame, has READ and WRITE modes, is granted by pgbuf_fix or a watcher, ends at the matching unfix, and never gives row or class ownership or transaction isolation. The transaction lock, owned by the lock manager, protects a logical object such as a class or row OID, uses modes such as IX_LOCK, is acquired through lock_object, ends under the transaction protocol rather than at unfix, and never gives safe access to page bytes. A bottom box shows that heap insert holds both on different objects, and the footer states that holding either does not imply holding the other.
svg.text: Two protections, two objects, two lifetimes
One heap insert needs both. Solid border: page buffer. Dashed border: lock manager.
PAGE LATCH · page buffer
Protects
the resident bytes of one BCB and its frame
Modes
READ shares with readers; WRITE excludes everyone
Granted by
pgbuf_fix(), or a PGBUF_WATCHER wrapped around it
Ends
at the matching unfix: one fix debt, page-scoped
Never gives
row or class ownership, or transaction isolation
Question it answers: who may read or change these bytes right now?
TRANSACTION LOCK · lock manager
Protects
a logical object: the class or the row OID
Modes
for example IX_LOCK on the class; the row-lock protocol
Acquired by
lock_object() and heap's own lock helpers
Ends
under the transaction protocol, not at unfix
Never gives
safe access to page bytes
Question it answers: which transaction may own or see this object?
heap_insert_logical() holds both, on different objects
class IX_LOCK and the row-lock protocol come from the lock manager;
the WRITE latch and its fix debt come from the home-page watcher
Holding either does not imply holding the other.
